lessons.title: Planning and preparing for pork classification
lessons.html:
Why pork carcasses are classified

In South Africa, pork carcasses sold through abattoirs are classified so that the buyer and the producer speak the same language about what the carcass is worth. Classification is controlled under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 and its regulations. A pig farmer delivering a load of baconers to the abattoir is paid according to the mass and class of each carcass, so a classifier's decision directly affects the money the farmer receives in ZAR. That is why the work must be accurate, consistent and honest.

Pork is classified mainly on lean meat content, using the PORCUS system. The classes run from P (the leanest) through O, R, C and U to S (the fattest). Lean meat content is estimated from measurements of back fat thickness and muscle thickness taken on the hot carcass with an approved instrument. Always work from the current regulations and the class tables supplied by your assignee or abattoir, not from memory.

Planning the shift

  • Check the slaughter schedule: how many pigs, which producers, and the expected line speed.
  • Confirm you are a registered classifier and that your registration is current.
  • Check the classification point on the line: good lighting, a safe standing platform, and space to reach the carcass without leaning over moving equipment.
  • Confirm that carcass identification (producer tattoo or slap mark, carcass number) will be readable at your station.

Preparing equipment

  • Grading probe: clean it, check the battery and cable, and do the calibration or zero check required by the manufacturer and your procedure. Record the check.
  • Roller marks and ink: use only approved food-grade marking ink. Make sure you have the correct class rollers and that they are clean and legible.
  • Recording system: check that the computer or data sheet links readings to the right carcass number.

Hygiene and safety

Wear clean protective clothing, a hairnet, gumboots and, where required, a cut-resistant glove and chain-mail apron. Wash and sanitise hands and the probe tip as your hygiene plan requires, because the probe enters the meat and can carry contamination from carcass to carcass. Watch for moving hooks, overhead rails and wet floors. Never reach into the path of the moving line, and know where the line stop button is.

lessons.title: Performing the classification
lessons.html:
Taking the measurements

Each carcass is measured at the point set out in the regulations and your procedure, normally on the back near the last ribs, a set distance from the midline of the split carcass. Your trainer and the procedure will show you exactly where. Taking the reading at the wrong place is the most common cause of a wrong class, so be consistent on every carcass.

  1. Check the carcass number and producer identification before you probe.
  2. Look at the carcass for anything that must be noted: bruising, damage, abscesses or trimming done by meat inspection.
  3. Insert the probe straight, at right angles to the skin, at the correct point. Hold it steady until the reading is taken.
  4. Read the back fat thickness and muscle thickness. The instrument or system calculates the estimated lean meat percentage.
  5. Check that the reading makes sense. A very lean reading on an obviously fat carcass means something went wrong; probe again.
  6. Clean the probe tip as required before moving to the next carcass.

Assigning the class

The lean meat percentage places the carcass in one of the PORCUS classes. Mass is also recorded, because buyers pay differently for porkers, baconers and heavier pigs. Use the class table from the current regulations; do not round readings in the producer's favour or against them.

ClassMeaning
PHighest lean meat content
O, R, C, UDecreasing lean meat content
SLowest lean meat content (fattest)

Problems on the line

  • If the probe gives an error or impossible reading, stop and re-check calibration.
  • If the carcass cannot be measured properly (for example badly damaged at the measuring point), follow your procedure for unclassified or specially marked carcasses and tell your supervisor.
  • If the line runs too fast for accurate work, ask for it to be slowed. Accuracy comes before speed.

Never classify a carcass you did not measure, and never change a class because a producer or buyer asks you to. Classification must be independent.

lessons.title: Completing the classification process
lessons.html:
Marking the carcass

Once the class is confirmed, the carcass is marked with the class mark using the approved roller and food-grade ink, in the position set by your procedure. The mark must be clear and complete so that the butcher, retailer and inspector can read it. A smudged or missing mark creates disputes and can mean the carcass has to be held back.

Recording and reporting

Every classification result must be recorded against the correct carcass number and producer. The records are used to pay the farmer and to give feedback on how the pigs are performing. A farmer who sees many carcasses in the fatter classes can change feeding, genetics or slaughter mass. Good records therefore help the whole pork chain.

  • Check that the number of carcasses classified matches the number slaughtered for each producer.
  • Record any carcasses that were not classified, re-probed or specially marked, with the reason.
  • Record equipment checks and any faults found during the shift.
  • Hand records to the abattoir office or upload them as required, and keep copies as your procedure says.

End of shift

  1. Clean the probe and roller marks according to the hygiene plan, and store them in a clean, dry place.
  2. Do a final calibration or check if your procedure requires it, and report any instrument that is not working correctly.
  3. Leave the classification point clean and safe for the next shift.
  4. Report any problems, such as unreadable identification, line speed issues or disputes, to your supervisor.

Handling disputes

Sometimes a producer questions a class. Stay calm and professional. Show the recorded reading and explain how the class was assigned. If there is a formal dispute process through the assignee, follow it. Your best protection is accurate measurement, correct marking and complete records.

Key points

  • Pork is classified under the PORCUS system on estimated lean meat content, from P (leanest) to S (fattest).
  • Calibrate and clean the probe before work, and measure at the same correct point on every carcass.
  • Check carcass identification before measuring, and re-probe readings that do not make sense.
  • Mark carcasses clearly with approved food-grade ink and record every result against the right carcass.
  • Classification must be independent: never change a class because someone asks you to.

quiz.question: Which classification system is used for pork carcasses in South Africa?

options.text: The A, AB, B, C age system

quiz.question: What is pork classification mainly based on?

options.text: The farm the pig came from

quiz.question: In the PORCUS system, which class has the highest lean meat content?
The probe gives a very lean reading on a carcass that is clearly fat. What should you do?

options.text: Accept the reading because the instrument is always right
Probe again and check calibration if the problem continues
Skip the carcass without recording it

quiz.question: What kind of ink must be used to mark the class on a carcass?

options.text: Spray paint used for marking pigs on the farm

quiz.question: A classifier may change a carcass class if the producer asks politely.
The probe tip should be cleaned between carcasses because it can carry contamination from one carcass to the next.
Which of these should be done when completing the classification at the end of a shift? (select all that apply)

options.text: Check that the number classified matches the number slaughtered per producer
Clean and store the probe and roller marks
Throw away records of re-probed carcasses
Report faulty instruments to the supervisor
Leave the probe on the floor to dry
